newsitem.title: TURKEY: Clock ticking for Turkey's ruling Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Clock ticking for Turkey's ruling Islamists.

text.p: Time appears to be running out for Turkey's first Islamist-led government, locked in a damaging dispute with the secularist military over religious activism.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's conservative coalition partners decided late on Wednesday to withdraw from the government unless its leader Tansu Ciller was made prime minister within a week, party officials said.
"This government has stopped being effective," the Hurriyet daily on Thursday quoted Ciller as telling her True Path Party.

"Unless the premiership is handed over to Tansu Ciller by June 18, the party's decision-making body will meet to decide to withdraw from the government," party deputy chairman Mehmet Gozlukaya was quoted as saying by the state-run Anatolian news agency.

However, Turkish law requires the president and later parliament to approve any alteration in government, and it remains uncertain the coalition, now lacking a clear majority, could see through any such change.

Ciller, the pro-Western foreign minister, had announced earlier in the day that there would be a change of government within days to resolve the split with the military that has brought the coalition to breaking point.
The True Path decision came only hours after the powerful military called on ordinary Turks to fight the danger of Moslem activism.

"It is the main duty of every secularist and democratic citizen who loves his country...not to stand neutral and to act against the increasing reactionary threat," General Fevzi Turkeri said at an army briefing for reporters on resurgent Islamism.

The secularist army and Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party have been engaged in a political firefight since February when a military-dominated security council ordered a crackdown on religious activity in public life.

Ciller and Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist leader, announced on June 1 that they would seek early elections to overcome the dispute. Under the plan, Erbakan would hand over power to Ciller who would head a caretaker government to prepare for elections.
Temel Karamollaoglu, a leading Welfare member, said on Wednesday that polls were expected to take place in October and a parliamentary decision to go for early elections would be taken this month.

But opposition parties and analysts said early elections before an upgrade of electoral rolls, which should be carried out after October 26 by law, were not possible and suggested they take place in March, 1998.
Officials from the High Election Board have said they need at least six to eight months from October to complete the upgrade of the rolls.
At Wednesday's briefing, the military said Iran was playing a role in the spread of Islamist activism in Turkey.
"Iran is providing every kind of support to build a regime in Turkey based on the principles of sharia (Moslem holy law)," Turkeri said.

Erbakan has sought to foster links with Iran since coming to power last June, but the secularist establishment has continued to protest at what it sees as Iranian support for separatist Kurdish rebels fighting in Turkey.
